description: Remove repeated integer values from an unsorted singly linked list. Keep the first original node for each distinct value and retain those nodes in their original order. Change links in the existing list, preserve every node's Value, and return no value. The original head remains the head, unless the list was empty.
constraints: The list is finite and acyclic, with 0..2000 nodes and signed 32-bit values.
Do not allocate replacement result nodes. Removed nodes remain owned by the caller; C++ must not delete them.
Example arrays show node values in head-to-tail order. The judge checks original node identities as well as values.
why: A set answers whether the current value already has a retained occurrence. Only a duplicate must be bypassed; keeping a pointer to the last retained node makes that link change possible without searching backward.
correctness: Before each step, the retained prefix contains exactly the first occurrences in the processed original prefix, in order. The set contains precisely those values. A new value extends both the set and retained prefix. An existing value is bypassed without advancing the retained predecessor. These cases preserve the invariant and, at exhaustion, retain exactly the required original nodes.
walkthrough: For original nodes [6,2,6,3,2], retain the first 6 and the first 2. Bypass the second 6, retain 3, then bypass the final 2. The reachable original nodes have indices [0,1,3] and values [6,2,3].
time: O(n) expected time with hash-set operations; pathological hashing can make the worst case O(n^2).
space: O(u) auxiliary space for u distinct values, at most O(n). No replacement list is allocated.
edges: Empty and one-node lists.
All values equal keeps only the original head.
Nonadjacent duplicates and negative values.
related: remove_duplicates_from_sorted_list requires sorted input, so it is not an alias for this unsorted exercise.

description: Return the existing node that is kth from the tail of a singly linked list, counting the tail as k=1. Return null/None/nullptr if k is nonpositive or exceeds the list length. Preserve every Value and Next link. Return the node object itself, not a copied node or its integer value.
constraints: The list is finite and acyclic with 0..2000 nodes and signed 32-bit values; k is any signed 32-bit integer.
The example output is the selected node's zero-based index in the original list, or null when there is no such node. That index is an adapter observation, not the callable's return type.
Equal values in different nodes remain different objects.
why: Moving a lead pointer k links ahead creates a fixed k-link gap. Advancing both pointers together preserves that gap; when the lead falls off the end, the trailing pointer has exactly k nodes including itself left to the tail.
correctness: Nonpositive k cannot name a one-based position. If the lead reaches null before k advances, the list is too short. Otherwise the lead stays exactly k links ahead of the trailing pointer throughout the joint walk. At termination its position is one past the tail, so the trailing pointer is exactly kth from the tail and is an original node. No links or values are changed.
walkthrough: For [4,7,7,9] and k=2, advance the lead from index 0 to index 2. Joint steps move the pair to (3,1), then (null,2). Return the original node at index 2, whose value is 7; the equal-valued node at index 1 is not the answer.
time: O(n) time, including out-of-range k: the lead walk stops at null rather than performing k unchecked steps.
edges: Empty input and all nonpositive k return null.
k=1 selects the tail; k=n selects the head.
Repeated values require identity-sensitive grading.

description: Given only a reference to a node in a singly linked list, remove that position's value without access to the head or predecessor. If target is nonnull and has a successor, copy its successor's value into target and bypass that successor, then return true. For a null target or the tail, return false without changing anything. The target object itself remains alive and remains the node reached from its predecessor.
constraints: A supplied target belongs to a finite acyclic list with 0..2000 nodes and signed 32-bit values, or is null.
The normal exercise uses an internal node. The defined failure cases also cover null and a tail node; no sentinel node may be appended.

Preserve every original object. Only target.Value and target.Next may change. In particular, an external alias to the bypassed successor still observes its original value and link. C++ must not delete caller-owned nodes.
Examples provide [listValues,targetIndex] to the adapter; only the selected node is passed to DeleteMiddle. Index -1 denotes null. The observed output contains success and reachable values.
why: Without a predecessor reference, the incoming link to target cannot be changed. Moving the successor's payload into target removes the requested value from the reachable sequence while allowing target's own outgoing link to bypass the now-redundant successor object.
correctness: If target has a successor S, replacing target.Value with S.Value and target.Next with S.Next changes the local sequence [targetValue,SValue,...] into [SValue,...]. The predecessor still reaches the same target object; every other object retains its fields. A tail has no successor to supply a replacement, so this technique cannot delete it, and returning false preserves the list.
walkthrough: In [8,4,7,2], target is the original index-1 object containing 4. Copy 7 into that object and point it to the original node containing 2. Reachable values become [8,7,2] and success is true. An alias to the original index-2 node still sees its value 7 and its original successor.
time: O(1) time once the target reference is supplied. Adapter list construction is not part of the callable cost.
space: O(1) auxiliary space; no replacement nodes are allocated.
edges: Null and tail targets fail without mutation.
Equal target and successor values still require the successor to be bypassed.
External successor aliases must remain valid.

description: Rearrange a singly linked list so that every node with Value < pivot comes before every node with Value >= pivot. Return the new head. Reuse each original node exactly once and preserve its Value. Either relative order within a partition is allowed; stability is not required. Do not create a cycle or allocate replacement result nodes.
constraints: Input is a finite acyclic list of 0..2000 nodes; values and pivot fit signed 32 bits.
Values equal to pivot belong to the second partition, mixed freely with larger values. This is a two-way partition, not a three-way partition.
The displayed output is one valid ordering. Tests accept every ordering satisfying the partition and node-identity rules.
why: Separate head/tail pointers for the two partitions let each node be appended to its proper side in constant time. Detach a node before appending it so old links cannot retain nodes in the wrong side or form cycles.
correctness: After each original node is processed, the two temporary lists contain disjoint processed original nodes, exactly partitioned by the comparison, with unchanged values. Appending the current node to the corresponding tail preserves this property. Joining the first list's tail to the second list's head places all smaller nodes before all remaining nodes and contains every original node exactly once. Empty sides are handled by returning the other head.
walkthrough: For [5,1,4,2,4,0] with pivot 4, appending to the two sides builds [1,2,0] and [5,4,4]. Joining them yields [1,2,0,5,4,4]. An unstable implementation may return another ordering; either 4 may appear before 5 within the second side.
time: O(n) time with one pass and constant-time tail appends.
space: O(1) auxiliary space; only a fixed number of node pointers is kept.
edges: Empty input and either partition being empty.
All values equal to the pivot belong to the second side.
Repeated values require a node multiset/identity check, not only value counts.

description: Add two nonnegative integers encoded as singly linked lists of decimal digits. Return their sum as newly allocated digit nodes in the same digit order. When mostSignificantFirst is false, the head is the units digit; when true, the head is the highest-place digit. Support both orders, covering the forward-order extension of the exercise. Preserve all input values and links, and do not share result nodes with either input.
constraints: Each input is finite and acyclic with 0..2000 digit nodes, each Value in 0..9. Inputs share no nodes.
An empty input denotes zero. If both inputs are empty, return null. Otherwise return a nonempty representation, including [0] for zero.
A nonempty input has no leading zero in the selected numeric order unless it is the single node [0]. The result must obey the same rule.
Do not convert the complete operands to a fixed-width integer. The mathematical sum may have thousands of digits.
Examples list digit values in head-to-tail order; the boolean argument selects their interpretation.
why: Carry propagation starts at the units column. Reverse-order lists already expose that column first. Forward-order lists require access from their tails, so stacks of digits provide the same units-first processing without modifying the inputs. Each column contributes sum % 10 and a carry sum / 10 to the next column.
correctness: After processing k low-order columns, the emitted digits equal the low k decimal digits of the operand sum, and the carry is exactly the amount owed to the next column. Adding the next available digits (or zero for an exhausted operand) preserves this invariant by quotient/remainder division by ten. Processing a final carry completes the sum. Appending in reverse-order mode or prepending in forward-order mode places each generated digit in the declared output order. Every output node is newly allocated and input links are only read.
walkthrough: For forward-order [4,9] and [5,8], the operands are 49 and 58. The units column gives 9+8=17, so emit 7 with carry 1. The tens column gives 4+5+1=10, so emit 0 and carry 1. Prepending the final carry gives [1,0,7]. The same sum in reverse order uses [9,4] and [8,5] and returns [7,0,1].
time: O(n + m) time for operand lengths n and m, including a possible final carry.
space: O(1) auxiliary space in reverse-order mode, excluding the new result; O(n + m) auxiliary space for digit stacks in forward-order mode. The result has at most max(n,m)+1 nodes.
edges: Both empty; one empty; single-digit zero.
A carry propagating through all columns adds a leading digit.
Unequal lengths and both digit orders.
Input identity and disjoint newly allocated result nodes.
related: int_as_list_add covers reverse-order addition only; it cannot stand in for both required digit orders.
title: Sum Lists

csharp.signature: LinkedListNode? AddLists(LinkedListNode? first, LinkedListNode? second, bool mostSignificantFirst)

python.signature: def AddLists(first: LinkedListNode | None, second: LinkedListNode | None, mostSignificantFirst: bool) -> LinkedListNode | None
python.solutionCode:
def AddLists(
    first: LinkedListNode | None, second: LinkedListNode | None, mostSignificantFirst: bool
) -> LinkedListNode | None:
    if mostSignificantFirst:
        left, right = [], []
        current = first
        while current is not None:
            left.append(current.Value)
            current = current.Next
        current = second
        while current is not None:
            right.append(current.Value)
            current = current.Next
        result, carry = None, 0
        while left or right or carry:
            total = carry + (left.pop() if left else 0) + (right.pop() if right else 0)
            result = LinkedListNode(total % 10, result)
            carry = total // 10
        return result
    dummy = LinkedListNode(0)
    tail = dummy
    p, q, carry = first, second, 0
    while p is not None or q is not None or carry:
        total = carry
        if p is not None:
            total += p.Value
            p = p.Next
        if q is not None:
            total += q.Value
            q = q.Next
        tail.Next = LinkedListNode(total % 10)
        tail = tail.Next
        carry = total // 10
    return dummy.Next

description: Return whether a singly linked list's integer values read the same from head to tail as from tail to head. Preserve every original node, Value and Next link. An empty list is a palindrome.
constraints: Input is finite and acyclic with 0..2000 nodes; values fit signed 32 bits.
The result compares values, not node identities. The preservation requirement still applies on both true and false exits.
why: Copying values into an auxiliary sequence gives direct access to mirrored positions without modifying singly linked links. Comparing only the first half tests each required mirrored pair once.
correctness: The auxiliary sequence is exactly the original head-to-tail value sequence because each node is read once in order. A sequence is a palindrome exactly when positions i and n-1-i are equal for every i below n/2. Rejecting the first unequal pair or accepting after all these comparisons implements that condition. The traversal never writes any node field, so every exit preserves the input.
walkthrough: For [3,8,1,8,3], copy the five values. Compare positions 0 and 4 (3=3), then positions 1 and 3 (8=8); the middle 1 needs no partner. Return true. Replacing the final value by 4 makes the first comparison fail, without changing a link.
time: O(n) time for traversal and mirrored comparisons.
space: O(n) auxiliary space for the copied values.
edges: Empty, one-node, even-length, and odd-length lists.
Repeated values alone do not guarantee a palindrome.
Early rejection must preserve all original links.
related: is_list_palindromic requires a per-language mutation-contract review before reuse; this entry explicitly preserves the list.

description: Return the first node object shared by two acyclic singly linked lists, or null if they share no node. Intersection means object identity, not equal integer values. Once two lists share a node, their following suffix is the same chain. Preserve all node values and links.
constraints: The union has at most 4000 original nodes, all with signed 32-bit values; either head may be null.

Examples provide [firstPrivatePrefix,secondPrivatePrefix,sharedSuffix] to the adapter. Equal values in the two private prefixes create separate objects. The shared suffix is allocated once and attached to both prefixes.
The displayed result is the returned node's zero-based index in the first list, or null. The callable itself returns the existing shared node object.
why: A pointer traversing first then second and another traversing second then first cover the same combined length. Switching heads after reaching null cancels any difference in private-prefix lengths without measuring them or changing a link.
correctness: Let private-prefix lengths be a and b and shared-suffix length c. If the pointers have not already met, their two-list routes reach the shared entry after the same a+b+c link advances and one head-switch step, so they meet at that entry, not merely an equal-valued node. Equal private-prefix lengths may make them meet earlier at that same entry. With no shared suffix, both routes have equal total length and end at null. Comparisons use object identity and the algorithm only reads links, so it returns exactly the first common node and preserves the lists.
walkthrough: For private prefixes [4,4] and [4], followed by the one shared suffix [9,2], the lists have lengths 4 and 3. Their first three 4-valued objects are separate. Head switching aligns the pointers at the shared 9 node, whose index in the first list is 2. Return that object, not either private 4 node.
time: O(n + m) time for list lengths n and m.
edges: Disjoint equal-valued lists must return null.
One or both null heads; identical heads; one head already inside the other list's suffix.
A one-node shared suffix and very unequal private-prefix lengths.

description: Return the original node where a singly linked list's reachable cycle begins, or null if following Next eventually reaches null. Preserve every Value and Next link. Equal values in different nodes do not establish a cycle.
constraints: There are 0..2000 original reachable nodes with signed 32-bit values. The tail either points to null or to one of those nodes; no other graph edges exist.
Examples provide [values,cycleIndex] to the adapter, which links the last node to that zero-based index. Index -1 means no cycle. The callable receives only head.
The displayed output is the original entry node's zero-based index, or null. Return the node itself, not that index, a boolean, or a copied node.
why: A fast pointer gains one position per step on a slow pointer inside a cycle, guaranteeing a collision. Their first collision is generally not the cycle entry. Resetting one pointer to the head and then advancing both at equal speed removes the prefix offset and locates the entry.
correctness: If the fast pointer or its next link reaches null, there is no cycle. Otherwise let the noncyclic prefix have length mu and the cycle length lambda. At collision, slow has traveled t steps and fast 2t, so t is a multiple of lambda. The collision's cycle offset is therefore -mu modulo lambda. A pointer reset to the head reaches the entry after mu steps, while the other advances from that offset by mu and also reaches the entry. Before that point the reset pointer lies in the noncyclic prefix, so this is their first meeting. No field is written.
walkthrough: For values [6,1,6,4,8] and cycleIndex=2, the tail returns to the original second 6 node. With prefix length 2 and cycle length 3, the pointers first collide inside the cycle. Reset one to index 0 and take equal steps; after two steps both reach original index 2. Return that original object, despite the equal-valued head.
time: O(n) time in the number of reachable original nodes: detection and entry alignment each use a linear number of advances.
edges: Empty and acyclic lists return null.
Self-loop, cycle at the head, and a long prefix before a short cycle.
Repeated payloads must not be mistaken for repeated node identities.
related: blind75_linked_list_cycle returns only a boolean and is not a replacement for the required entry-node result.
